introduction: On this fifth Sunday of Lent, Jeremiah announces a new covenant, written not on stone but on the heart. In the Gospel, some Greeks ask to see Jesus, and he answers by speaking of the grain of wheat that must fall into the earth and die to bear fruit. His hour has come. In many places, crosses and images are now veiled until Good Friday. Let us draw near to the one who, lifted up from the earth, draws all people to himself.

prayerOfTheFaithful.invitation: Brothers and sisters, the Lord has promised to write his law in our hearts. Let us pray to him with trust.
intentions: For the Church: that she may help all who come to her, saying, we want to see Jesus, to meet him in her life and worship. Let us pray to the Lord.
For persecuted Christians and all who suffer for their faith: that, like the grain of wheat, their witness may bear much fruit. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those who are afraid of suffering or of death: that they may find courage in Christ, who was troubled and yet trusted his Father. Let us pray to the Lord.
For catechumens who will be baptized at Easter: that the Lord may give them a new heart and a steadfast spirit. Let us pray to the Lord.
For ourselves: that in these last days of Lent we may let go of whatever keeps us from following Jesus. Let us pray to the Lord.
prayerOfTheFaithful.conclusion: Faithful God, you promised a new covenant written on our hearts. Create in us a clean heart, and draw us close to your Son as he goes to his Passion. Through Christ our Lord.

reflection.title: The grain of wheat
reflection.body:
The prophet Jeremiah lived through the collapse of everything his people trusted: the king, the city, the temple. Yet in that darkness God gives him a promise: a new covenant. "I will put my law in their inward parts, and I will write it in their heart." No one will need to be taught to know the Lord, because "I will forgive their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more." The psalm turns that promise into a prayer: "Create in me a clean heart, O God."

In the Gospel, some Greeks come to Philip with a simple request: "Sir, we want to see Jesus." Jesus does not invite them to a meeting. He speaks of his death: "unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit." If they want to see him, they will have to look at the cross.

Jesus does not hide his anguish. "Now my soul is troubled." He could ask to be spared, but he chooses another prayer: "Father, glorify your name!" The Letter to the Hebrews describes the same struggle: he prayed "with strong crying and tears," and "learned obedience by the things which he suffered."

Then Jesus makes a promise that reaches every nation, including those Greeks: "And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself."

The grain of wheat is a pattern for our lives too. Something in us has to fall into the ground and die: a grudge, a fear, a comfortable habit, our need to be in control. It feels like loss. Jesus promises it is the way to fruit. As we enter the last two weeks before Easter, ask him which grain you need to let fall, and trust him with the harvest.
